newsitem.title: USA: Passenger jet fleet to double by 2014 - McDonnell.
newsitem.headline: Passenger jet fleet to double by 2014 - McDonnell.

text.p: The world's passenger jet fleet will need to double in the coming 20 years, adding 13,600 aircraft worth an estimated $1.1 trillion, according to a report published this week by McDonnell Douglas Corp.
The need for new planes will be driven by rising global passenger traffic, which is expected to rise 5.9 percent annually in the next 20-years, the report said.

Rapidly expanding economies in the Asia/Pacific region, with the fastest projected traffic growth of any region at 8.1 percent a year, will allow that market's fleet to leap-frog over Europe into second place behind the North American fleet.

The report predicts the majority of the new aircraft needed will be short- and medium-range narrowbody aircraft, with demand for widebody jets gaining momentum over the length of the forecast. It also said:
-- North America will need 4,700 new planes, 34 percent of the total, and will account for half of the demand for narrowbody jets because of extensive domestic service.
-- Asia/Pacific will need 3,900 new units, with heavy demand for widebody aircraft meaning that region will have to spend $445 billion, or 40 percent of total global expenditures.
-- Europe will see the slowest growth in traffic, needing 3,300 deliveries valued at some $250 billion.
Freight is expected to grow faster than passenger traffic, with global tonne-kilometers seen expanding at a clip of 7.4 percent annually.
The report predicts a 7.9 percent rise in cargo carried on air freighters and 6.9 percent annually on passenger planes.

The active freight fleet will grow to 2,720 airplanes from about 1,200 jets -- although most of that growth will be met by conversions of older passenger planes, with new models filling a secondary role, the report said.

The projections are underpinned by the assumptions that the global economy will grow some 3.3 percent annually, with no real increases in jet fuel prices expected. The report is based on 1995 dollar values and covers the period 1995 through 2014. Airlines from the former Soviet Union are excluded due to lack of available data.
